title: Questioning is not a thing.
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles takes aim at the school habit of spending years on 'improving questioning' through wait time, hinge questions, exit tickets and the rest of a baker's dozen of techniques. His objection is that this approach improves one teacher at a time, forever, and ties up leadership attention in a skill that is not among the most important things in a subject. He proposes that departments instead centralise the work: plan spaced retrieval questions, design tasks, collect excellent examples of student work and build shared assessments in a common curriculum so that individual classroom skill matters less. He then picks on hinge questions as his test case, arguing that a single hinge question for something like essay writing is nearly impossible to write, and that asking students to explain how an excellent essay beats a standard one reveals misconceptions while teaching far more.
points: Treating questioning as a separate school-wide improvement priority is a slow, one-teacher-at-a-time approach to CPD.
Retrieval questions, tasks and assessments can be designed once by the department and taught by everyone, so classroom questioning skill is not the bottleneck.
Hinge questions are hard to write for complex skills such as essay writing and give a narrow view of student thinking.
A comparison task, asking students how a grade 8/9 essay differs from a grade 5/6 one, surfaces misconceptions and teaches at the same time.
quotes: Most people don’t call this a gift! This is why I spend most of my time pointing people to data and research. Let them smell the bovine mess for themselves.
But I feel this approach only improves one teacher at a time, forever and ever. Amen. It is a bovine approach to CPD.

Hinge questions, exit tickets, application questions, Blooms … these are only a means to finding out what a student can do. So instead the team should focus on task design, which goes into a centralised curriculum which everyone teaches. Individual classroom skill is not required.
Leaders will rarely have to check a teacher’s skill in any of these. Why? Because they will be jointly created and, in the centralised curriculum, all teachers will use them.

So now our training can be much more useful, because it will develop the curriculum. This will dramatically improve teachers’ knowledge, which is easy. It won’t require a massive increase in skill, which would be both hard and time consuming.

Give the student two essays, each using the same quotes, answering the same question. One is standard - grade 5/6. The other is excellent - grade 8/9. Then ask just one question: “How is the excellent essay better than the standard (apart from being longer)? Write your answer with at least 5 explanations.
Students will still reveal their misconceptions. But they will also learn a tremendous amount at the same time - how many other misconceptions will be dispelled?
